messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Tane is a 63-year-old publisher who came to treatment after years of trying to manage on his own following a man-made disaster at an industry event. He had been attending an evening reception connected to a book fair, the kind of professional gathering where conversation clustered around small tables and drinks were constantly being poured. He remembers the scene in striking visual fragments: the shine of bottles behind the bar, people turning toward a sudden disturbance, the sharp disorganization of the room when panic broke out. What stayed with him was not a blurred impression but a series of crisp, intrusive images that still arrive unbidden, as if the event were stored as pictures rather than a story he can place in the past. Even now, if he tries to speak about what happened, he can feel the memory push forward on its own, clear and detailed in ways he never asked for.

In the weeks after, Tane found that the memory did not wait for him. He would wake from a nightmare and, before he was fully oriented to his bedroom, the same images would force their way back into his mind. The smell of alcohol was especially potent because it took him straight back to the reception, to the bar area and the sense that danger had erupted in an ordinary social setting. Being asked about the event by colleagues or family was no better; the act of talking about it seemed to pull the pictures closer and sharpen them. He came to dread these moments because he knew how quickly they could turn into a full reliving of the scene.

What frightened Tane most was how little safety he felt anywhere afterward. He had come to believe that danger could break into even familiar places without warning, and he noticed that he was on guard even inside his own home. Ordinary sounds made him jump—a dropped utensil in the kitchen, a car door outside, the crack of something falling in his office—and the startled surge in his body left him feeling ashamed and exposed. In that state of constant readiness, the memories seemed even more accessible. The more jumpy and watchful he felt, the more easily the event returned in those vivid visual bursts, as though his mind were continually searching for the same threat and finding it in the past.

He responded by organizing his life around vigilance. In restaurants, meetings, and even in his own conference room at the publishing house, Tane always chose a seat with his back to the wall so he could monitor the whole room. He scanned entrances, watched people’s hands, tracked abrupt movements, and avoided seeing friends if he thought the gathering would involve a bar or casual questions about where he had been that night. These habits made sense to him as precautions; he felt he would be foolish not to stay alert. But living this way kept him braced for danger, and the constant checking made the world feel more threatening rather than less. He noticed he was startling more easily and feeling tense at home, as if his own strategies were teaching him that nowhere was truly safe.

The same habits also kept the event mentally alive. By repeatedly surveying rooms and positioning himself defensively, Tane found himself mentally comparing every setting to the reception where the disaster occurred. Entering a crowded launch party for one of his authors, he would immediately look for walls, exits, and signs of trouble, and the old images would rush back with painful clarity. Avoiding friends narrowed his life and reduced the ordinary conversations that might have grounded him in the present; instead, the disaster remained a sealed, highly visual pocket in his mind, ready to intrude. Even his effort not to be caught off guard by waking from nightmares turned into a kind of dread at bedtime, because mornings often began with the memory already pressing in.

At work this has become increasingly costly. As a publisher, he is expected to host authors, attend receptions, and move easily through crowded literary spaces, yet he now arranges himself at the edge of rooms and spends more energy scanning than listening. He has turned down social dinners with colleagues and skipped gatherings with friends, telling himself he is tired or busy. His wife has watched him check locks, react sharply to small noises, and insist on sitting where he can see every entrance, even in their own home. Tane finally sought help after waking from another nightmare and finding that the memory would not loosen its grip for the rest of the day; at a meeting later that morning, the smell of wine from a catered event and a routine question about the disaster left him shaken and mute. He says he is tired of living as if the event is still happening, but he is afraid that if he stops guarding himself, something catastrophic will catch him unaware again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes intrusive memories and later avoidance/vigilance, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that the memory itself leads Tane to use maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers bringing back the memory, but does not state that the memory causes or generates triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette describes maladaptive strategies and mentions trigger-like situations, but it does not explicitly convey in the same paragraph that those strategies lead to or create triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What stayed with him was not a blurred impression but a series of crisp, intrusive images that still arrive unbidden, as if the event were stored as pictures rather than a story he can place in the past. Even now, if he tries to speak about what happened, he can feel the memory push forward on its own, clear and detailed in ways he never asked for.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because the pictures came back with so little warning, Tane began trying to manage his days around them, steering away from conversations, rooms, and routines that might give the images a foothold and keeping himself deliberately guarded whenever he could not avoid them.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He would wake from a nightmare and, before he was fully oriented to his bedroom, the same images would force their way back into his mind. The smell of alcohol was especially potent because it took him straight back to the reception, to the bar area and the sense that danger had erupted in an ordinary social setting.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After enough mornings like that, the memory seemed to spread outward into the rest of his life, attaching itself to more and more ordinary cues—the scent of wine at lunch meetings, a colleague's casual question, the hum of a crowded reception—until he felt there were reminders waiting almost everywhere.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He responded by organizing his life around vigilance. In restaurants, meetings, and even in his own conference room at the publishing house, Tane always chose a seat with his back to the wall so he could monitor the whole room.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Over time, these precautions created their own landscape of reminders: any room where he had to think first about walls, exits, or whether alcohol would be served began to feel marked by the disaster before anything had even happened.
<<<END>>>
